description: Maya, the Lokas, the Trimurti, prakriti and purusha, the trigunas and the Mahayuga cycle.
content_html:
The Material World and Maya

In Hindu cosmology, the world we experience is real but not the deepest level of reality. The concept of maya describes the veil of illusion that makes the material universe appear to be the final truth. Maya is not simply a lie; it is the creative power that produces the appearance of multiplicity out of the one Brahman. The Chandogya Upanishad (III 14) teaches that “all this is Brahman” — yet maya causes ordinary perception to see only the surface of things.

The Nasadiya Sukta, found in the Rig Veda, is one of Hinduism’s oldest reflections on the nature of existence. It meditates on what was present before creation — “neither being nor non-being existed” — and acknowledges the profound mystery of how anything came to be at all. This philosophical humility is characteristic of Hindu cosmology, which holds multiple accounts of creation together rather than insisting on a single narrative.

Prakriti and Purusha

Hindu Samkhya philosophy offers a systematic account of the material world through the concepts of prakriti and purusha. Prakriti is primordial matter: the raw substance from which everything in the universe — including human minds, emotions and intellect — is produced. Purusha is pure consciousness, the unchanging witness. The Bhagavad Gita (XIII 19–20) states that both prakriti and purusha are without beginning; prakriti is the cause of all action and production, while purusha is the cause of experiencing pleasure and pain.

The confusion of purusha with prakriti is seen as the root of spiritual bondage: when consciousness mistakenly identifies with the material processes of body and mind, it becomes caught up in samsara. Liberation, in Samkhya thought, comes from clearly discriminating between the two — recognising that the witnessing consciousness is not the same as the material world it observes.

Key Fact

Prakriti is primordial matter (including mind and intellect); purusha is pure consciousness. The Bhagavad Gita (XIII 19–20) teaches that prakriti is the cause of all action, while purusha is the cause of experience. Mistaking one for the other is the source of bondage.

The Three Gunas: Qualities of Matter

Prakriti operates through three fundamental qualities called the trigunas. The Katha Upanishad (III 10–11) and the Bhagavad Gita describe how these three qualities are woven into everything that exists:

  • Tamas — inertia, darkness, heaviness and resistance to change. Associated with ignorance and lethargy.
  • Rajas — energy, passion, desire and restless activity. Associated with ambition and attachment to results.
  • Sattva — purity, clarity, lightness and harmony. Associated with wisdom and spiritual insight.

Everything in the material world, including human personalities, food, environments and actions, is a mixture of these three gunas in different proportions. Spiritual progress is understood partly as a movement from tamas and rajas towards sattva, and then beyond even sattva to pure purusha (consciousness).

Hindus may use the gunas as a framework for understanding their own behaviour and making choices. Tamasic behaviour includes sleeping too much, eating heavy or stale food, and avoiding responsibility. Rajasic behaviour includes competitive striving and emotional volatility. Sattvic behaviour includes eating fresh food, cultivating calmness and pursuing learning. The Bhagavad Gita encourages a life that cultivates sattva as a preparation for deeper insight, while recognising that all three gunas are part of maya and must ultimately be transcended.

The Lokas: Realms of Existence

Hindu cosmology describes a universe of many realms, known as Loka (world or realm). These realms are not simply spatial locations but modes of existence. The beings who inhabit them include Devas — divine, luminous beings who enjoy great powers — and Asuras — powerful but spiritually darkened beings associated with ego and desire. The human realm is considered a rare and valuable birth because it is one of the few from which liberation (moksha) can be achieved directly.

The heavenly realms of the Trimurti are particularly significant. Brahma-Loka is the realm of the creator deity Brahma; beings there enjoy enormous lifespans but eventually return to rebirth when that karma is exhausted. Shiva-Loka is the realm of Shiva and is associated with deep spiritual energy and the prospect of liberation for devoted worshippers. Vishnu-Loka, also called Vaikuntha, is the eternal realm of Vishnu, described in Vaishnava tradition as a place of permanent liberation and loving devotion.

Key Fact

Rebirth into any of the Lokas — including the heavenly realms of Brahma-Loka, Shiva-Loka and Vaikuntha — is determined by karma. Even heavenly existences are temporary unless full liberation is achieved, though Vaikuntha (Vishnu-Loka) is understood by Vaishnavas as a realm of permanent liberation.

Aum and the Cyclical Universe: The Mahayuga

Hindu cosmology is cyclical rather than linear. Time itself moves in vast cycles called Mahayuga, each composed of four ages or yugas of decreasing spiritual quality — from the golden age (Satya Yuga) through the Treta and Dwapara Yugas to the present Kali Yuga, an age of spiritual decline. Each Mahayuga lasts 4,320,000 years; at the end, the universe is dissolved (pralaya) and then re-created. This cycle of creation and dissolution is overseen by the three members of the Trimurti: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer and regenerator. The sacred sound aum is understood as the primordial vibration that underlies and pervades all of creation.

Hindu traditions differ on how literally to understand the cosmological accounts. Some schools treat the lokas, yugas and the Trimurti’s cosmic roles as profound symbolic truths rather than literal geography and history. Others, particularly in devotional (bhakti) traditions, regard the descriptions as real cosmic realities. The Advaita school reads cosmology through the lens of maya: all multiplicity — the many lokas, the many deities, even the cyclical universe — are expressions of one Brahman, ultimately non-dual. Both interpretations are found within living Hindu traditions.
exam_tip_html: Questions about Hindu cosmology often require you to use precise terminology: ‘prakriti’, ‘purusha’, ‘trigunas’, ‘Mahayuga’, ‘Vaikuntha’. A common mistake is confusing maya (the veil of illusion) with the idea that the world does not exist — Hinduism does not teach that; it teaches that the world is real but not ultimate. For the 15-mark Discuss, show awareness that Hindu traditions disagree on cosmology (literal vs symbolic; Advaita non-dualism vs Vaishnava devotional realism). Accurate spelling of specialist vocabulary (including ‘sattva’, ‘tamas’, ‘rajas’) gains SPaG credit.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hindu cosmology describes the material world as real but pervaded by maya (illusion); prakriti (matter) and purusha (consciousness) are the two eternal principles, and confusion between them is the root of spiritual bondage.
  • The trigunas — tamas, rajas and sattva — are the three qualities woven through all material existence; spiritual progress involves cultivating sattva and ultimately transcending all three.
  • The universe moves through vast cyclical Mahayugas governed by the Trimurti (Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva); rebirth into heavenly Lokas is determined by karma, though Vaikuntha (Vishnu-Loka) is understood by Vaishnavas as a realm of permanent liberation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'Loka' in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: A world, realm or plane of existence in Hindu cosmology. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Hindu understanding of the trigunas.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the three fundamental qualities of prakriti/matter; tamas (inertia/darkness), rajas (energy/passion) and sattva (purity/clarity); everything in the universe is a mixture of these three; spiritual progress involves moving from tamas and rajas towards sattva. [2 marks — 1 for naming the gunas or giving a simple description, 2 for a more developed account]

practice_questions.text: Outline the roles of the Trimurti in the cycle of creation and destruction.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: the Trimurti consists of Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver) and Shiva (destroyer/regenerator); the universe moves through vast cycles called Mahayugas; at the end of each Mahayuga the universe is dissolved (pralaya) and then re-created; Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains and Shiva destroys in preparation for a new cycle; each figure has a corresponding realm (Brahma-Loka, Shiva-Loka, Vishnu-Loka/Vaikuntha). [3 marks — 1 for naming the Trimurti, 2 for explaining two roles, 3 for a full account including the Mahayuga cycle]

practice_questions.text: Explain the Hindu concepts of prakriti and purusha and their relationship to spiritual liberation.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prakriti is primordial matter from which all physical and psychological realities emerge; purusha is pure consciousness or spirit; both are described in Bhagavad Gita XIII 19-20.
• When purusha mistakenly identifies with prakriti, it becomes bound in samsara; liberation comes from clearly discriminating between the two.
• The trigunas are the three qualities of prakriti (tamas, rajas, sattva) woven through all material existence; spiritual progress moves towards sattva and then beyond all three gunas.
• The Katha Upanishad (III 10-11) describes the hierarchy of realities rising from the senses through the mind to purusha.
[6 marks — 3 marks per concept: 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed explanation with a source of wisdom]

practice_questions.text: 'The cyclical view of the universe in Hinduism makes human life meaningless.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that could support the statement: if the universe endlessly cycles through creation and dissolution, individual lives may seem insignificant on a cosmic scale; the Kali Yuga (current age) is described as spiritually degenerate, which could produce pessimism; the vastness of the Mahayuga (4,320,000 years) dwarfs human existence.

Arguments that could challenge the statement: the human realm is described as rare and precious because moksha can be achieved from it; karma gives every action genuine moral weight and consequence; the cyclical universe is not fatalistic — individual choices in the present (kriyamana karma) always matter; bhakti traditions emphasise loving relationship with God (Vishnu/Vaikuntha) as giving life deep personal meaning; the Nasadiya Sukta's humility before mystery can inspire awe rather than nihilism; dharma (duty) structures meaningful engagement with life at every stage.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita XIII 19-20; Nasadiya Sukta; Katha Upanishad III 10-11), explicit weighing of arguments and a justified conclusion.
Secure: two clear perspectives with some use of Hindu teaching; conclusion present.
Developing: one side more developed; some relevant content; limited source use.
Emerging: one-sided or very brief; little specific Hindu content.

practice_questions.text: Outline what Hindus believe about the Devas and Asuras.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: Devas are divine, luminous beings who enjoy great powers and inhabit higher realms; Asuras are powerful beings associated with ego, desire and spiritual darkness; both are part of the many-realm (Loka) cosmology of Hinduism; people can be born into realms inhabited by Devas or Asuras as a result of karma; even Deva existence is temporary unless moksha is achieved. [3 marks — 1 for identifying Devas/Asuras, 2 for contrasting them, 3 for linking their existence to karma and the wider cosmological picture]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the three gunas is associated with purity, clarity and spiritual insight?
What is Vaikuntha in Hindu cosmology?
options: The realm of Brahma where beings live until their karma is exhausted
The primordial sound underlying all creation
The realm of Vishnu understood by Vaishnavas as a place of permanent liberation
The present age of spiritual decline in the Mahayuga cycle

knowledge_checks.q: The two eternal principles in Samkhya philosophy are prakriti (matter) and _____ (pure consciousness).
The Nasadiya Sukta, which meditates on what existed before creation, is found in the _____.
Match each member of the Trimurti to their cosmic role:
right: Destroyer and regenerator at the end of each cycle

flashcard_questions.q: What is maya in Hindu cosmology?
flashcard_questions.a: The creative illusion that conceals Brahman and makes multiplicity appear real.
Primordial matter; the source of all physical and psychological realities.
Pure consciousness or spirit, distinct from all material processes.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three gunas and give a one-word quality for each.

flashcard_questions.a: A great cycle of cosmic time made up of four ages, ending in dissolution and re-creation.
The eternal realm of Vishnu, described in Vaishnava tradition as a place of permanent liberation.
Divine, luminous beings with great powers who inhabit higher realms in Hindu cosmology.
Powerful beings associated with ego and desire, contrasted with the luminous Devas.

flashcard_questions.q: Which ancient Vedic hymn reflects on the mystery of existence before creation?
Which guna is associated with spiritual decline and is said to characterise the present Kali Yuga?
According to Bhagavad Gita XIII 19-20, what is prakriti the cause of?
flashcard_questions.a: All action and production in the material world.

flashcard_questions.q: Which member of the Trimurti governs the dissolution of the universe at the end of a Mahayuga?

glossary_terms.definition: Illusion or the creative power that produces the appearance of a separate, material world, concealing the ultimate reality of Brahman.
The primal matter or material nature from which all physical and psychological realities emerge.
Pure consciousness or spirit; the witnessing self that is distinct from all material processes.
The three fundamental qualities of prakriti: tamas (inertia), rajas (energy/passion) and sattva (purity/clarity).
A world, realm or plane of existence; Hindu cosmology describes multiple lokas inhabited by different kinds of beings.
A great cycle of time in Hindu cosmology, made up of four yugas (ages); the universe is created and dissolved repeatedly across such cycles.
